evidence.title: Festuca
evidence.text: Festuca (fescue) is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the grass family, Poaceae (subfamily Pooideae).

evidence.title: Festuca
evidence.text: They are evergreen or herbaceous perennial tufted grasses with a height range of 10 - and a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on every continent except Antarctica.

evidence.title: Festuca
evidence.text: The genus is closely related to ryegrass ("Lolium"), and recent evidence from phylogenetic studies using DNA sequencing of plant mitochondrial DNA shows that the genus lacks monophyly.

evidence.title: Festuca
evidence.text: As a result, plant taxonomists have moved several species, including the forage grasses tall fescue and meadow fescue, from the genus "Festuca" into the genus "Lolium".

evidence.title: Diocirea
evidence.text: Diocirea is a genus of flowering plants in the figwort family, Scrophulariaceae.

evidence.title: Diocirea
evidence.text: The genus is endemic to a small area in the south-west of Western Australia and is intermediate in character between "Eremophila" and "Myoporum".

evidence.title: Diocirea
evidence.text: There are four members of the genus, all of which are small shrubs with stems and leaves which produce a resin making the plants appear bluish-green.

evidence.title: Diocirea
evidence.text: Neither the genus, nor any of the species had been described before 2007 although a few specimens had been collected as "Eremophila elachantha".

evidence.title: Diocirea
evidence.text: Despite their limited distribution, they often occur in populations of several thousand individual plants, forming a dense ground cover.

evidence.title: Cussonia
evidence.text: Cussonia is a genus of plants of family Araliaceae, which is native to the Afrotropics.

evidence.title: Cussonia
evidence.text: It originated in Africa and has its center of distribution in South Africa and the Mascarene Islands.

evidence.title: Cussonia
evidence.text: Due to their striking habit, they are a conspicuous and easily recognizable group of plants.

evidence.title: Cussonia
evidence.text: Their genus name commemorates the botanist Pierre Cusson.

evidence.title: Cussonia
evidence.text: The Afro-Malagasy and Asian "Schefflera", and Afrotropical "Seemannaralia" genera are related taxa that share several of its morphological characteristics, among which the leaves borne on the end of branches, inflorescences carried on terminal branches or stems, and reduced leaf complexity in developing inflorescences.

evidence.title: Luzula
evidence.text: Luzula is a genus of flowering plants the family Juncaceae, the rushes.

evidence.title: Luzula
evidence.text: The genus has a cosmopolitan distribution, with species occurring throughout the world, especially in temperate regions, the Arctic, and higher elevation areas in the tropics.

evidence.title: Luzula
evidence.text: Plants of the genus are known commonly as wood-rush, wood rush, or woodrush.

evidence.title: Luzula
evidence.text: Possible origins of the genus name include the Italian "lucciola" ("to shine, sparkle") or the Latin "luzulae" or "luxulae", from "lux" ("light"), inspired by the way the plants sparkle when wet with dew.

evidence.title: Luzula
evidence.text: Another etymology sometimes given is that it does derive from lucciola but that this meant a midsummerfield, or from the Latin luculus, meaning a small place; the same source also states that this name was applied by Luigi Anguillara (an Italian botanist) in 1561.

evidence.title: Cerceris
evidence.text: Cerceris is a genus of wasps in the family Crabronidae.

evidence.title: Cerceris
evidence.text: It is the largest genus in the family, with over 1030 described species.

evidence.title: Cerceris
evidence.text: The genus has a cosmopolitan distribution, with species on every continent.

evidence.title: Myosotidium
evidence.text: Myosotidium is a genus of plants belonging to the family Boraginaceae.

evidence.title: Myosotidium
evidence.text: This genus is represented by the single species Myosotidium hortensia, the giant forget-me-not or Chatham Islands forget-me-not, which is endemic to the Chatham Islands, New Zealand.

evidence.title: Myosotidium
evidence.text: The biogeography is yet unresolved, but its ancestors are likely from the American continent, as "Myosotidium hortensia" was found to be sister to the South American plant genus "Selkirkia" and both genera being sister to the North American genus "Mimophytum".

evidence.title: Owenia (plant)
evidence.text: Owenia is a genus of plants, mainly trees in the mahogany family Meliaceae.

evidence.title: Owenia (plant)
evidence.text: They are endemic to Australia and fairly widespread across the continent.

evidence.title: Owenia (plant)
evidence.text: There are five species in the genus, most from New South Wales and living in conditions ranging from wet rainforest to the verges of the desert.

evidence.title: Owenia (plant)
evidence.text: Like many plants, it plays its part in patch dynamics.

evidence.title: Ternstroemia
evidence.text: It is distributed in tropical and subtropical regions in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: Eugenia is a genus of flowering plants in the myrtle family Myrtaceae.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: It has a worldwide, although highly uneven, distribution in tropical and subtropical regions.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: The bulk of the approximately 1,000 species occur in the New World tropics, especially in the northern Andes, the Caribbean, and the Atlantic Forest (coastal forests) of eastern Brazil.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: Other centers of diversity include New Caledonia and Madagascar.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: Many species new to science have been and are in the process of being described from these regions.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: For example, 37 new species of "Eugenia" have been described from Mesoamerica in the past few years.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: At least 20 new species are currently in the process of being described from New Caledonia, and approximately the same number of species new to science may occur in Madagascar.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: Despite the enormous ecological importance of the myrtle family in Australia (e.g. "Eucalyptus", "Corymbia", "Angophora", "Melaleuca", "Callistemon", "Rhodamnia", "Gossia"), only one species of "Eugenia", "E. reinwardtiana", occurs on that continent.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: The genus also is represented in Africa south of the Sahara, but it is relatively species-poor on that continent.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: In the past some botanists included the morphologically similar Old World genus "Syzygium" in "Eugenia", but research by Rudolf Schmid in the early 1970s convinced most botanists that the genera are easily separable.

evidence.title: Eugenia
evidence.text: Research by van Wyk and colleagues in South Africa suggests the genus may comprise at least two major lineages, recognizable by anatomical and other features.

evidence.title: Nymphaea
evidence.text: Nymphaea is a genus of hardy and tender aquatic plants in the family Nymphaeaceae.

evidence.title: Nymphaea
evidence.text: The genus has a cosmopolitan distribution.

evidence.title: Nymphaea
evidence.text: Many species are cultivated as ornamental plants, and many cultivars have been bred.

evidence.title: Nymphaea
evidence.text: Some taxa occur as introduced species where they are not native, and some are weeds. Plants of the genus are known commonly as water lilies.

evidence.title: Nymphaea
evidence.text: The genus name is from the Greek νυμφαια, "nymphaia" and the Latin "nymphaea", which mean "water lily" and were inspired by the nymphs of Greek and Latin mythology.
